title: Management of orchards
competency: Plan orchard planting, calculate plants per hectare from spacing, and choose suitable irrigation practices and methods.

en.text: An orchard is land used only for fruit; it needs planning, resources and a long time to establish. Site selection is the most important decision, because the site affects yield, quality and marketability. Land is prepared and holes dug: in good soil with irrigation a 30 × 30 cm or 50 × 50 cm hole 80–100 cm deep. Topsoil and subsoil are kept apart; topsoil is mixed with mature manure or decomposed coffee husk. Seedlings are planted without breaking or bending the tap root.

ideas.name: Planting distance and plants per hectare

en.text: Spacing depends mainly on the fruit crop (big mango trees or small banana and papaya plants), the variety's canopy width, the propagation method (seedlings grow larger), and soil quality and rainfall. Plants per hectare = 10 000 m² ÷ (row spacing × plant spacing). Apples at 3 m × 2 m give 10 000 ÷ 6 ≈ 1667 trees per hectare; mango at 10 m × 10 m gives 100.

opts: The spacings must be multiplied: 6 m² per tree, so about 1667 trees
screens.ans: The spacings must be multiplied: 6 m² per tree, so about 1667 trees

screens.ask: Project 2.1: a school plot is 12.4 m long and 10 m wide. Papaya rows run 3.1 m apart along the length, plants 2.4 m apart across. Whole plants that fit = ___
screens.why: 12.4 ÷ 3.1 = 4 rows. 10 ÷ 2.4 = 4.17, so 4 plants per row (whole plants only). 4 × 4 = 16 plants.
screens.clue: Round each count DOWN to whole plants.

screens.ask: The book prints 1324 passion-fruit plants per hectare. With plants 3.3 m apart, what row spacing would give about 1324? Row spacing ≈ ___ m (1 decimal place)
screens.why: Area per plant = 10 000 ÷ 1324 = 7.55 m². Row spacing = 7.55 ÷ 3.3 = 2.29 ≈ 2.3 m. So 1324 does not fit 3.3 m × 4.0 m.
screens.clue: Work backwards: area per plant = 10 000 ÷ plants.

en.text: Irrigation applies controlled amounts of water to help grow crops, landscape plants and lawns, and has been practised for over 5,000 years. The grower must check water quality (salt content), the amount and the timing; both too much and too little water reduce yields. Irrigating in the morning or late afternoon reduces evaporation loss. When rainfall is not enough, supplementary irrigation is used.

en.text: Surface (gravity) irrigation such as basin, flood and furrow applies water directly to the soil surface; it is cheap, easy and needs no technology or skill and suits low infiltration soils, but needs accurately levelled land, does not suit high infiltration soils and wets plants unevenly. Pressurized systems apply water through pipes: sprinklers spray water like rain, suit high infiltration soils and unlevelled land and allow fertigation, but are costly, suffer wind drift and need power and enough water; drip delivers water drop by drop at the root zone, saving water and allowing fertigation, but has high maintenance cost and is uneconomical for closely spaced crops.

screens.title: Surface (gravity) irrigation
paras: Water is applied directly to the soil surface: basin, flood or furrow.
Advantages: easy to maintain, low cost, no modern technology, no technical skill.
Works well on soils with a low infiltration rate.
Disadvantages: land must be levelled accurately.
Not suitable for soils with a high infiltration rate.
Plants are covered with water even when not needed; some spots get too much.
No drainage outlet.
screens.note: The book writes "filtration rate"; the correct term is infiltration rate.

screens.title: Pressurized irrigation
paras: Water under pressure flows through pipes.
It applies water more effectively than surface irrigation.

Sprinkler: water is sprayed into the air and falls like rain. Suits high infiltration soils and unlevelled fields; fertigation is possible. But costly, wind drift, needs continuous power and enough water.
Drip: water falls drop by drop at the root zone. Saves water, keeps the root zone moist, fertigation is possible. But high maintenance cost; not economical for closely spaced crops.

notes.text: Table 2.1: passion fruit 3.3 m × 4.0 m gives 10 000 ÷ 13.2 ≈ 758 plants/ha, not 1324 as printed. The lesson teaches 758. Also "Pasion" → Passion, "Mannual" → Manual, and the cited SNV source is a vegetable, root and tuber manual.

p.36: "The whole" should be "The hole". The hole-filling instructions do not say which material fills each level, and a 30 × 30 cm hole 80–100 cm deep is an unusual shape (many guides use about 60 × 60 × 60 cm). Check with a subject teacher.

p.37: "filtration rate" should be "infiltration rate" (corrected in the lesson). There is no heading 2.6.1; irrigation lettering is inconsistent (two "a." items). Figure 2.8 shows a vegetable crop, not fruit.

Added (marked): 1 ha = 10 000 m², the plants-per-hectare formula, the Figure 2.7 worked example, the slider, the Project 2.1 plot item and the comparison table of irrigation methods. Fertigation and infiltration rate are defined here; the book uses them without definition.
